clinicalPearls: The great majority of childhood constipation is functional, with no underlying organic disease
A cycle of painful or hard defaecation leads to stool withholding, progressive rectal loading, and faecal impaction
Overflow, or paradoxical, soiling is the involuntary leakage of loose stool around impacted faeces and may be mistaken for diarrhoea
Withholding behaviour such as posturing, stiffening, and hiding is frequently misinterpreted by parents as straining to pass stool
Diagnosis is clinical using symptom-based Rome criteria, and onset often coincides with weaning, toilet training, or starting school

Red flags such as delayed passage of meconium, onset in the neonatal period, faltering growth, or abnormal neurological or spinal findings prompt evaluation for organic causes such as Hirschsprung disease
Digital rectal examination and routine imaging are not needed in straightforward cases

Management combines disimpaction followed by maintenance osmotic laxatives with behavioural measures such as a regular toileting routine, adequate fluid and fibre, and demystification, continued long enough to break the cycle
reference.pathophysiology: Painful defaecation prompts the child to withhold stool voluntarily. Retained stool becomes harder, larger, and more difficult to pass, while the rectum distends and gradually accommodates the growing mass so that the sensation and urge to defaecate diminish. Liquid stool then leaks around the impacted faeces, producing overflow soiling. This self-reinforcing cycle perpetuates the constipation in the absence of any structural or organic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Spinal cord abnormality such as a tethered cord or spina bifida occulta
Metabolic causes such as hypercalcaemia, or medication side-effects
additionalInvestigations: Clinical, Rome-based diagnosis from history and examination, which is usually sufficient
Coeliac serology and thyroid function tests if an organic cause is suspected
Abdominal examination and, selectively, imaging to assess faecal loading in difficult cases
Neurological and spinal examination, with spinal imaging if neurological signs are present
Rectal biopsy for Hirschsprung disease when red flags are present
Calcium and other metabolic tests where clinically indicated
Review of diet, fluid intake, and drug history
redFlags: Delayed passage of meconium beyond the first day or two of life, or constipation from birth
Abdominal distension with vomiting suggesting obstruction
Abnormal neurological examination or spinal or sacral abnormalities
Ribbon-like stools, or an empty rectum with a palpable abdominal faecal mass suggesting Hirschsprung disease
reference.prognosis: The outlook is good with early, adequate, and sustained treatment, and many children recover, but under-treatment or premature withdrawal of laxatives commonly leads to relapse and prolonged symptoms.
pitfalls: Under-dosing or stopping maintenance laxatives too early and causing relapse
Mistaking overflow soiling for diarrhoea and withholding treatment
Omitting disimpaction before starting maintenance therapy
Missing red flags for Hirschsprung disease or a spinal cause
Relying on behavioural advice alone without adequate laxative therapy
references: Rome diagnostic criteria for paediatric functional gastrointestinal disorders
